report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false**—for *prescription, purified cannabidiol* used **as an add-on** to existing antiseizure medicines in children with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome.

Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials found fewer convulsive seizures with cannabidiol. In the 2017 trial (120 patients aged 2–18), the FDA label describes a 20-mg/kg/day cannabidiol group versus placebo; this evidence supported approval for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome. [https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf)

A subsequent 199-child trial found convulsive-seizure frequency fell **48.7%** with 10 mg/kg/day and **45.7%** with 20 mg/kg/day, versus **26.9%** with placebo over 14 weeks. [https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458)

A systematic review/meta-analysis limited to randomized placebo-controlled trials likewise evaluated CBD as adjunctive treatment in Dravet syndrome and found benefit, rather than evidence of no effect. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32040850/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32040850/)

Important qualifications: this does **not** mean cannabis products or over-the-counter CBD are proven substitutes; the trials used standardized pharmaceutical cannabidiol, alongside other medicines. Benefit is incomplete and variable—not seizure cure—and adverse effects and drug interactions (notably sedation and liver-enzyme elevations, especially with valproate) require specialist monitoring.
